docs.title: QMaxent Manual
docs.text: Welcome to the QMaxent user manual. QMaxent integrates the elapid Python library into QGIS to deliver the full Maxent species distribution modeling (SDM) workflow — training, spatial cross-validation, jackknife variable importance, projection, and survey planning — through a familiar bilingual interface.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
If this is your first visit:

  1. Read Introduction for the 2-minute orientation
  2. Install the plugin → Installation
  3. Set up Python dependencies → Dependencies
  4. Download the bundled example data → Example datasets
  5. Walk through your first model in 5 minutes → Quick start

If you already use QMaxent and want to dig into a specific feature, the User guide chapters mirror the plugin's five tabs one-for-one. Each can be read on its own.

If you want to see the tool put through its paces on real datasets, the Worked examples cover three case studies of increasing complexity, including a reproduction of the Lee et al. (2025) fairy pitta study published in Global Ecology and Conservation.

docs.title: Conventions used in this manual
docs.text:
• Bold marks UI labels (buttons, tabs, menu items) you click.
  • monospace marks file paths, code, and parameter values you type.
  • Numbered tabs (①, ②, …) refer to the QMaxent Analysis dock tabs.
  • Inline citations like (Phillips et al. 2017) point to entries in the References chapter.
  • Sidebar boxes flag warnings (⚠), tips (💡), and notes worth a second glance — but most of the manual is plain prose; we do not use boxes decoratively.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text: If you use QMaxent in your research, please cite the software using the metadata in the repository's CITATION.cff. The same metadata is rendered live on the project home page at osgeokr.github.io/qmaxent and in the References chapter of this manual.

docs.title: The Analysis dock
docs.text: The QMaxent Analysis dock is the heart of the plugin. It organises the entire SDM workflow into five numbered tabs that you progress through in order, left to right. This chapter is a quick tour of the layout; each tab then has its own detailed chapter.

docs.title: Opening the dock
docs.text: Choose Plugins → QMaxent → QMaxent Analysis. The dock opens on the right side of the QGIS main window by default and can be detached, floated, or re-docked using the standard QGIS panel handles.

docs.title: The five tabs at a glance
docs.text:
# Tab Purpose Detailed chapter ① Data Pick or load presence points (point file or CSV); register environmental rasters; pre-flight raster grid and CRS check ① Data tab ② Parameters Choose feature classes, regularization, spatial CV scheme, output paths ② Parameters tab ③ Training Live progress bar and log while the model fits ③ Training tab ④ Results Response curves, Jackknife importance, spatial projection ④ Results tab ⑤ Survey Site Selection Turn the prediction into field-ready candidate survey sites ⑤ Survey Site Selection

The numbered glyphs are deliberate: even when QGIS is configured in a language other than English, the order is unambiguous.

docs.title: Status bar
docs.text: A persistent status bar at the bottom of the dock shows the most recent run summary — presence count, background count, training AUC, and CV AUC. It is updated continuously as you click around, so you can switch projects or reopen QGIS and immediately see whether the dock is showing a fresh state or a previous run's results.

docs.title: Persistence across QGIS sessions
docs.text: QMaxent remembers your last-used presence layer, raster set, parameter values, and output paths inside the QGIS project file (.qgz). When you reopen a project, the dock reflects the previous state — no need to re-pick layers each time.

docs.title: Buttons across the bottom
docs.text:
The footer of the dock has three persistent buttons:

  • ▶ Run Maxent — start a training run
  • ▶ Run Spatial Projection — apply the trained model across all rasters
  • ▶ Select Survey Sites: sample candidate survey sites from the prediction

These buttons are enabled only when their prerequisites are met: e.g. projection becomes available only after a model has been trained, and survey site selection requires a projection raster on disk.

docs.title: What this means for your workflow
docs.text: The dock's design encodes the canonical Maxent workflow described in Elith et al. 2011: assemble inputs → choose hyperparameters → fit → evaluate → project → act. By making each stage a separate tab with its own status, QMaxent forces a discipline that helps catch the silent failures Roberts et al. 2017 and Araújo et al. 2019 warn about — particularly raster mismatch and over-optimistic AUCs from non-spatial CV.

docs.title: ① Data tab
docs.text: The Data tab is where you tell QMaxent which species you are modeling and which environmental variables to use. Three controls deserve attention: the presence-points selector, the environmental-raster list with its Check Raster Consistency action, and the background-points sample size.

docs.title: Step 1. Choose the presence points
docs.text:
1. Presence Points Layer lists every point layer in the project. Choose your species layer. The grey line below it tells you how many points were loaded.
  2. Open point file... adds a point file (GeoPackage, shapefile, GeoJSON and other formats QGIS reads) to the project and selects it.
  3. Load CSV (X/Y columns)... reads a table with coordinate columns (see Step 2).

docs.title: Step 2. (Optional) Load presence points from a CSV table
docs.text:
1. File: the path of the table.
  2. Browse... chooses the file.
  3. Delimiter is detected for you. Change it only if the columns look wrong.
  4. X / longitude column: the longitude or easting column.
  5. Y / latitude column: the latitude or northing column. QMaxent guesses both from the column names (for example lon/lat, x/y).
  6. Coordinate reference system: the CRS of the numbers in the table. Use EPSG:4326 for decimal degrees.
  7. Click OK. The table is added to the project as a point layer.

docs.title: Step 3. Add the environmental rasters
docs.text:
1. Add from project puts every raster layer of the project in the list. Add raster files... adds rasters straight from disk.
  2. Each row has a type button. [continuous] is for measured amounts such as temperature; [categorical] is for class codes such as land cover or biome. Click the button to switch. Use Remove selected and the ▲ ▼ buttons to remove rows or change their order.

docs.title: Step 4. Check that the rasters line up
docs.text:
1. Click Check Raster Consistency.
  2. A green status line means every raster has the same CRS, extent and resolution. A red line means they differ; see Fixing rasters that do not line up.

docs.title: Step 5. Check the background points
docs.text:
1. Background Points: Sample count is the number of random background points (10,000 by default). See Background points below.
  2. Export for external Maxent is optional. It writes the same data for the Java Maxent program (see Export for external Maxent).

When these steps are done, go to the ② Parameters tab.

docs.title: Presence Points Layer
docs.text:
The first drop-down lists every loaded vector point layer in the current QGIS project. Pick the layer that contains your species occurrence records. QMaxent reads the geometry and reports the count beside the selector (e.g. 116 presence points loaded).

If the records are not in the project yet, two buttons below the drop-down load them without a detour through the QGIS menus. The new layer is added to the project and selected as the presence layer.

  • Open point file...: any point format QGIS can read (GeoPackage, Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML, GML, FlatGeobuf and others). A file that does not contain points is refused with a message.
  • Load CSV (X/Y columns)...: a delimited table with one row per record, for example a GBIF download. QMaxent detects the delimiter (comma, semicolon, tab or pipe) and suggests the longitude/latitude or X/Y columns from their names (for example decimalLongitude and decimalLatitude in GBIF files, or lon/lat, x/y). Check the suggested columns and choose the coordinate reference system of the coordinates. The default is EPSG:4326, which is correct for decimal-degree tables.

Tips for preparing this layer:

  • Geometry must be Point or MultiPoint. Lines and polygons must be converted to centroids first via Vector → Geometry Tools → Centroids….
  • CRS can be anything — QMaxent reprojects on the fly to match the raster grid. That said, a projected CRS that matches the rasters avoids a mid-run reprojection step.
  • Duplicates and clustering are tolerated but distort the model. maxent.jar keeps one presence per raster cell by default; QMaxent keeps all records, and the ③ Training tab log reports how many share a cell. Reduce the records to one per cell or apply spatial thinning before modeling (Boria et al. 2014), for example with the standalone tool spThin. Records with identical coordinates can also be removed with Vector → Geoprocessing Tools → Delete Duplicate Geometries.
  • Very large presence sets (hundreds of thousands of points) are usually dominated by such duplicates and need several GB of memory per model fit (about 4 GB for 100,000 points in our tests). Thin them first; the model rarely changes once each occupied cell is represented once.

docs.title: Environmental rasters
docs.text:
Two buttons populate the raster list:

  • Add from project: adds every raster layer currently loaded in the QGIS project. The fastest way to start.
  • Add raster files...: opens a multi-select file dialog for any single-band raster GDAL can read (GeoTIFF, ESRI ASCII .asc, .grd, ERDAS .img, VRT, NetCDF and others). The files are added to the QGIS project and to the list in one step.

The list follows the QGIS project: when a raster layer is removed from the project (or you open another project), its row disappears from the list and the status line asks you to run Check Raster Consistency again. Use the ▲ and ▼ buttons to change the order of the rows. The order matters for reproducibility, because background points are drawn from the first raster in the list (see Background points).

QMaxent uses one band per environmental variable. A multi-band raster (for example a stack of all bioclimatic variables in one file) is refused when you click ▶ Run Maxent, with the names of the affected files. Split it into single-band files first, for example with Processing > GDAL > Raster conversion > Rearrange bands (one band per output), then add the single-band files.

Each row in the raster list shows the file name and a [continuous] / [categorical] tag. Categorical detection is automatic when the file carries a PAM (.aux.xml) sidecar with the metadata key LAYER_TYPE=thematic. Without that tag, click the tag button of a row to switch it between [continuous] and [categorical].

Why categorical handling matters

Treating a categorical raster (e.g. biome, land-cover class) as continuous is one of the most common silent failures in operational SDM. Maxent will average across class codes as if they were ordinal, producing biologically meaningless responses. Always verify the [categorical] tag on integer-coded landscape rasters before training.

docs.title: Check Raster Consistency
docs.text:
This button runs the most important pre-flight check in the dock: do all rasters share the same CRS, extent, and resolution?

  • ✓ Pass (green): the stack is grid-aligned and ready to model.
  • ⚠ Mismatch (amber): one or more rasters disagree.
  • Unusable CRS: one or more rasters have a coordinate reference system that cannot be reprojected (see below).

When it fails, a second button — Harmonize to Folder… — appears. Clicking it lets you nominate an output directory; QMaxent reprojects every raster to the highest-resolution one in the stack (nearest-neighbour for categoricals, bilinear for continuous variables) and re-loads the harmonised set. The Ariolimax worked example walks through this in detail.

docs.title: Rasters with an unusable CRS
docs.text:
Some rasters cannot be aligned at all because of their CRS. The check reports two cases and names each affected file:

  • the raster has no CRS, or
  • the CRS is a local (engineering) system without a datum. This happens when a .prj file or GeoTIFF only carries the name of a projection, for example NAD83(NSRS2007) / Michigan South, and no datum. PROJ cannot transform such a CRS to any other CRS.

When the name matches an EPSG definition, the message suggests the matching EPSG code. To fix it, in the QGIS Layers panel right-click the raster, choose Layer CRS > Set Layer CRS..., select the correct CRS (for example the suggested EPSG code), and click Check Raster Consistency again. From then on, Check and Harmonize to Folder... use the CRS you set in QGIS for that raster. Alternatively, write a complete CRS into the file, for example with Raster > Projections > Assign Projection. Harmonize no longer stops with a raw PROJ error in this situation.

docs.title: Fixing rasters that do not line up
docs.text: The steps below use the Ariolimax Mismatch demo from Example datasets, whose rasters were changed on purpose.

docs.title: Step 1. Add the rasters and run the check
docs.text:
1. Choose the presence layer.
  2. Add the rasters with Add from project.
  1. Click Check Raster Consistency.
  2. Because the grids differ, a new button Harmonize to Folder... appears. Click it.
  3. The red status line names what differs (CRS, extent, resolution).

docs.title: Step 2. Choose a folder and let QMaxent align the rasters
docs.text: QMaxent asks for an output folder. It proposes a qmaxent_harmonized folder next to the first raster; click Select Folder to accept it. The original files are never changed. A progress window follows:

docs.title: Step 3. Replace the rasters in the list
docs.text:
1. Click Replace to use the aligned copies in place of the originals. Add as additional layers keeps both sets in the project.
  1. The list now points to the aligned copies.
  2. The status line turns green. You can continue to the ② Parameters tab.

docs.title: Background points
docs.text:
Maxent is a presence-background algorithm (Phillips et al. 2006; Fithian & Hastie 2013) — it contrasts presence locations against a background sample drawn from the rest of the study area. The default background sample is 10,000 points drawn at random from the valid (non-NoData) cells of the first raster in the list, the value Phillips & Dudík 2008 recommend for typical continental- to landscape-scale studies.

The draw is covered by Fix random seed on the ② Parameters tab: with the same seed, the same rasters in the same order and the same presences, every run uses the same background sample. (In v0.1.x the background was drawn anew on every run, even with a fixed seed.) Keep the raster order unchanged when you want to reproduce a run exactly.

You can override it in the Background points field. Smaller values are appropriate only for very small study areas (<10,000 cells); larger values rarely help and slow the run.

The Add presences to background checkbox is on by default — this is the convention the original Java MaxEnt applies and is required for the Maxent likelihood to be well-defined (Phillips & Dudík 2008).

docs.title: Export for external Maxent
docs.text:
This group writes your presence points and rasters in a form that the original Java program maxent.jar reads, so that you can run the same data there or share a ready-to-use Maxent input folder.

  1. The Export for external Maxent group.
  2. Samples + Raster writes a samples CSV and one .asc grid per raster.
  3. SWD writes two CSV files with the raster values already extracted at the presence and background points ("samples with data").
  4. Output folder: where the files go. Click ... to change it.
  5. Click Export. A README with an example maxent.jar command is written next to the files.

docs.title: Load existing model (.pkl)…
docs.text: The bottom of the tab has a Load existing model (.pkl)… button for re-using a previously trained model on new rasters. Picking a .pkl opens a variable-mapping dialog so you can re-state which raster maps to which saved variable name — a safeguard against silent ordering errors when collaborators use different file names. See Saving and reusing models for the full workflow and the security note on Python pickle files.

docs.title: Status line
docs.text: The bottom of the dock shows a one-line summary: presence=N background=M train AUC=… CV AUC=…. The AUC fields populate after the ③ Training tab finishes a run — they let you tell at a glance whether the dock state matches the most recent training.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
QMaxent's modeling engine — the elapid Python library and its companions (rasterio, geopandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib) — does not ship with QGIS. The first time you use the plugin, you install these dependencies into an isolated, per-plugin package folder so they do not affect your system Python or QGIS itself. On Linux and macOS this folder is a Python virtual environment; on Windows it is a plain package folder (see Where the packages are installed).

This is a one-time, ~5-minute setup.

docs.title: Step 1. Open the QMaxent Dependencies panel
docs.text:
The panel opens by itself right after the plugin is installed. You can also open it at any time from the menu.

  1. Open the Plugins menu.
  2. Point to QMaxent.
  3. Click QMaxent Dependencies.

docs.title: Step 2. Install the dependencies
docs.text:
1. Environment Status reads Dependencies not installed.
  2. Click Install / Update Dependencies.

The packages are downloaded from PyPI into ~/.qgis_qmaxent (%USERPROFILE%\.qgis_qmaxent on Windows), the path shown at the bottom of the panel. The download is about 300 to 500 MB (about 590 MB on disk). Allow 3 to 8 minutes on a typical broadband connection. A progress bar and the package being installed are shown below the button while you wait:

docs.title: Step 3. Check that the environment is ready
docs.text: 1. Environment Status turns green and reads ✓ QMaxent environment ready. You can close the panel and open QMaxent Analysis.

docs.title: Environment Status messages
docs.text: Message Meaning ✗ Dependencies not installed First-time setup needed ✓ QMaxent environment ready Everything is installed and ready to model ✗ Dependencies need updating The package list or the installation method changed with a plugin upgrade. Click Install / Update Dependencies again

docs.title: What is installed
docs.text:
QMaxent installs the following packages and their transitive dependencies:

  • elapid — the Maxent engine (maxnet algorithm, spatial cross-validation, projection); see Anderson (2023).
  • rasterio — raster I/O.
  • geopandas — vector I/O for presence points.
  • scikit-learn — cross-validation, ROC, AUC; see Pedregosa et al. (2011).
  • scipy + numpy — numerical core; see Harris et al. (2020).
  • matplotlib — response curves, ROC, jackknife plots.

These are pinned to versions that QMaxent has been tested against; the plugin's release notes record which versions ship with each release.

docs.title: Where the packages are installed
docs.text:
All dependencies go into one folder per QGIS Python version, inside ~/.qgis_qmaxent (%USERPROFILE%\.qgis_qmaxent on Windows). The folder name includes the Python version, for example venv_py3.12 for the Python 3.12 that ships with current QGIS releases.

Platform How the packages are installed Package location Windows The QGIS Python's own pip installs the packages into the QMaxent package folder (pip install --target). No separate Python interpreter is created. %USERPROFILE%\.qgis_qmaxent\venv_py3.12\Lib\site-packages Linux, macOS A Python virtual environment (venv) is created from the QGIS Python, and its pip installs the packages. ~/.qgis_qmaxent/venv_py3.12/lib/python3.12/site-packages

QMaxent only imports these packages inside QGIS, so on Windows it does not need an interpreter of its own. This change was made in 0.2.0: with QGIS 3.44.15 and later on Windows, the virtual-environment approach of 0.1.x stopped with "ensurepip ... returned non-zero exit status 1" before any package was downloaded.

Two environment variables change this behaviour. Set them before you start QGIS:

  • QMAXENT_CACHE_DIR: use another folder instead of ~/.qgis_qmaxent, for example when your home directory is not writable or has little free space.
  • QMAXENT_FORCE_VENV=1: on Windows, go back to the old virtual-environment method of 0.1.x. Use it only for troubleshooting.

docs.title: Remove Environment
docs.text:
Use Remove Environment to delete the entire QMaxent package folder (the virtual environment on Linux and macOS) from disk. You might do this to free disk space, force a fresh re-install when something is broken, or switch to a different QMaxent version that pins different package versions.

After removal, the status banner returns to Dependencies not installed and Install / Update Dependencies becomes available again.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Installation fails with a network or SSL error

Most often this is a corporate proxy or firewall blocking PyPI. Ask your administrator to allow pypi.org and files.pythonhosted.org. The installer respects QGIS's proxy settings, so configuring those in Settings → Options → Network usually fixes it.

Windows: 'ensurepip ... returned non-zero exit status 1'

You are running QMaxent 0.1.x with QGIS 3.44.15 or later. Upgrade the plugin to 0.2.0 or later, which installs the packages without a virtual environment on Windows, then click Install / Update Dependencies again.

Disk space exhausted during install

The installer needs roughly twice the final size as scratch space while extracting wheels. Free at least 1 GB on the drive that holds your home directory before retrying.

“No module named …” after a successful install

Restart QGIS once. Python's import cache occasionally needs a clean process to pick up the new environment.

Plugin starts but Run Maxent button is disabled

Open the Dependencies dialog and confirm the status is green. If it is, restart QGIS; if it is not, click Install / Update Dependencies again.

docs.title: Security note on the package folder
docs.text: QMaxent's package folder is populated only from PyPI, by the QGIS Python's pip on Windows and by a standard Python venv on Linux and macOS. The plugin does not execute arbitrary code from remote sources at runtime. Saved-model files (.pkl) are a separate concern; see Saving and reusing models for the security note on loading pickle files from untrusted sources.

docs.title: Example datasets
docs.text: QMaxent ships a one-click downloader for two canonical SDM example datasets, accessed from Plugins → QMaxent → Download Example Dataset... They are the same datasets the broader Maxent literature has used for almost two decades, which means you can compare your results directly with published benchmarks.

docs.title: Step 1. Open the downloader
docs.text:
1. Open the Plugins menu.
  2. Point to QMaxent.
  3. Click Download Example Dataset...

docs.title: Step 2. Choose a dataset and a folder
docs.text:
1. Choose the dataset. Bradypus variegatus is the best one to start with.
  2. Check Save to. The default is a qmaxent_examples folder in your home folder. Click ... to choose another folder.
  3. Click Download.

For Ariolimax, the dialog also offers a Variant:

  1. Select Ariolimax.
  2. Variant: Pre-harmonized (default) loads the rasters as published, all on one grid. Mismatch demo loads copies whose CRS, extent and resolution were changed on purpose, so that you can practise the raster consistency check (see Fixing rasters that do not line up).
  3. Save to works as for Bradypus.
  4. Click Download.

docs.title: Step 3. Wait for the download
docs.text:
1. The progress bar and the line below it show which file is being downloaded. Click Cancel to stop.

When the download ends, a message tells you where the files are:

  1. Click OK.

docs.title: Step 4. Check the layers
docs.text: 1. The presence layer and the environmental rasters are added to the Layers panel and drawn on the map. You can go straight to the Quick start.

docs.title: Bradypus variegatus dataset
docs.text:
The brown-throated three-toed sloth. This is the canonical Maxent test dataset published with Phillips, Anderson & Schapire (2006) and reused in virtually every subsequent Maxent paper.

Layer Description bradypus.shp 116 presence points across South and Central America bio1, bio5, bio6, bio7, bio8, bio12, bio16, bio17 WorldClim bioclimatic variables (continuous) biome Biome classification (categorical)

After download the layers appear immediately in the QGIS canvas:

The dataset is small (well under 100 MB) and the resulting Maxent runs typically finish in under 30 seconds, so it is ideal for first runs and for working through this manual.

docs.title: Ariolimax dataset
docs.text:
The Pacific banana slug. This is the default test dataset that ships with elapid.

Pre-harmonized or Mismatch demo?

The published Ariolimax rasters already share one CRS, extent and resolution, so Check Raster Consistency passes at once. Choose Mismatch demo in the Variant box when you want to see and fix a grid mismatch, as in the Ariolimax worked example. The demo copies are written to a mismatch_demo subfolder; the original files stay unchanged.

docs.title: Save location and project structure
docs.text:
Whichever dataset you choose, the downloader creates a sub-folder named after the species:

qmaxent_examples/
├── bradypus/
│   ├── bradypus.shp     (and .dbf, .shx, .prj, .cpg)
│   ├── bio1.tif         …
│   └── biome.tif
└── ariolimax/
    ├── ariolimax.shp
    └── …

Re-running the dialog with the same Save-to path overwrites previously downloaded files, so it is safe to use as a "reset to defaults" button if you want to start a tutorial cleanly.

docs.title: Loading the layers manually
docs.text: The plugin auto-adds layers, but if you ever need to reload them by hand, just drag the .shp and .tif files from QGIS's Browser panel into the Layers panel — exactly as you would for any other dataset.

docs.title: Where the data comes from
docs.text:
Both datasets are pulled from their canonical archival URLs at download time; QMaxent does not ship them inside the plugin itself. This keeps the plugin package small and ensures you always get the upstream-canonical version. If you need offline access, run the downloader once on a connected machine and copy the qmaxent_examples folder onto offline workstations.

Copies of both datasets are also kept in the example_data folder of the QMaxent repository (about 15 MB). The files are unchanged copies of the originals, and README.txt lists their sources and citations. Download the files and add the layers to a QGIS project.

docs.title: Exporting results
docs.text: Every QMaxent training run writes a multi-sheet XLSX workbook alongside the .pkl model. The workbook is intentionally formatted to read as a Supplementary Table block for an academic manuscript: Times New Roman, table-numbered headings, row footers explaining how each metric was computed. You can paste sheets directly into a paper's appendix.

docs.title: Output folder layout
docs.text:
After a training run that also produced a spatial projection and the Save analysis charts as PNG checkbox was on, the output folder looks like this:

File Produced by Use model.pkl Training Reload later via Load existing model (.pkl)… (Python pickle: open only trusted files) model_model_card.json Training Settings, data, performance, thresholds, importance and software versions; safe to share (see Saving and reusing models) model_coefficients.csv Training Every Maxent feature with feature type, variable, knot and coefficient; safe to share training_log.txt Training Copy of the training log prediction.tif Spatial projection Habitat-suitability raster prediction.tif.aux Spatial projection QGIS auxiliary metadata results.xlsx Training Multi-sheet supplementary table survey_sites.gpkg Survey Site Selection tab Field-ready candidate survey sites prediction_roc.png Spatial projection ROC curve (300 dpi) prediction_jackknife.png Spatial projection Jackknife bars (300 dpi) prediction_response_curves.png Spatial projection All response curves (300 dpi)

docs.title: Sheet-by-sheet description
docs.text: The XLSX has four to five sheets depending on which features you ran. The screenshots below are from a Pitta nympha run — the format is identical for every dataset; only the values change.

docs.title: Table 1 — Experimental setup
docs.text:
A one-page record of the full run configuration. Reviewers can verify seed, variable count, regularization, CV scheme, and training/CV AUCs at a glance. This is exactly the information Araújo et al. 2019 flag as the minimum methods-section reporting standard for a published SDM.

This sheet is the single best artefact for methods-section reproducibility. Cite it as your "Table S1" and a reader can re-execute the analysis bit-identically.

docs.title: Table 2 — Predictor variables
docs.text:
Lists every environmental variable, its type (continuous / categorical), and its training-data range. For continuous variables the range is [min, max]; for categorical, the discrete set of levels encountered during training.

Use this sheet to document extrapolation scope: any prediction applied to environmental values outside these ranges is by definition extrapolation (Elith, Kearney & Phillips 2010) and should be flagged in your results discussion.

docs.title: Table 3 — Cross-validation results
docs.text:
Per-fold held-out AUC and the across-fold mean ± standard deviation — the headline performance estimate.

Folds with degenerate test sets (e.g. all-positive after spatial partitioning) are reported as NaN and excluded from the mean. This matches the way the original Maxent literature handles the rare cases where a fold cannot produce a valid AUC.

docs.title: Table 4 — Jackknife variable importance
docs.text:
For each variable, four AUCs (only-train, only-test, without-train, without-test), plus a "Train AUC drop" and "Test AUC drop" column to make the contribution magnitudes scannable. Variables are sorted by descending Test AUC drop so the most uniquely-informative variables are at the top.

The footer note explains the drop columns: Drop = full-model AUC − without-variable AUC; larger drops indicate variables whose unique contribution is harder to recover from the others. This is the metric Phillips, Anderson & Schapire 2006 recommend as the most robust indicator of unique contribution.

docs.title: Survey sites
docs.text: The candidate sites from the ⑤ Survey Site Selection tab are written to their own GeoPackage (survey_sites.gpkg by default), not to the workbook. Its attribute table has one row per site with id, lat, lon, suitability, quartile and, when reverse geocoding was enabled, the OpenStreetMap address fields country, province, city_county, district and display_name. Open the attribute table in QGIS, or export it to a spreadsheet with Export > Save Features As..., if you need it as a supplementary table. See ⑤ Survey Site Selection for the field definitions.

docs.title: Customizing the export
docs.text:
The default file path on the ② Parameters tab is <home>/qmaxent_output/results.xlsx. Change it to anywhere writable; relative paths are resolved against the current QGIS project folder.

To stop the XLSX from being written (rare — usually faster to ignore the file than to disable it), simply clear the path field. QMaxent will skip the export and emit a notice in the training log.

The PNG analysis charts are controlled by the Save analysis charts as PNG checkbox on the ④ Results → Spatial Projection sub-tab. With it ticked, three additional PNGs are written next to the GeoTIFF at the moment you run projection. They are sized for direct paste into a single-column manuscript figure (300 dpi, ~1.6 MB each).

docs.title: Citing the workbook
docs.text:
The XLSX was designed to be cited the way published supplementary tables are cited:

Yu, B.-H. (2026). QMaxent results workbook for [Supplementary table]. https://github.com/osgeokr/qmaxent

If your model is reproducible (fixed seed + same input rasters) you can also distribute the model.pkl alongside the XLSX so reviewers can re-load the model and inspect predictions independently.

docs.title: FAQ & troubleshooting
docs.text: Common questions, error messages, and workarounds. If you do not see your issue here, please open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: "QMaxent environment not ready" stays red after install
docs.text:
Check the Plugins → QMaxent → Manage Dependencies dialog. If any of the required packages (elapid, numpy, scikit-learn, pandas, openpyxl) is reported missing, click Install missing.

If the dialog itself errors out, your QGIS Python may be missing pip. On Windows, run OSGeo4W Shell → python -m ensurepip --upgrade; on macOS/Linux, install QGIS via the OSGeo4W or Conda channel that ships with pip enabled.

docs.title: Windows: "ensurepip ... returned non-zero exit status 1"
docs.text: This error comes from QMaxent 0.1.x with QGIS 3.44.15 or later on Windows, where creating a Python virtual environment fails. QMaxent 0.2.0 installs the packages with the QGIS Python's own pip into the QMaxent package folder instead, without a virtual environment. Upgrade the plugin and click Install / Update Dependencies again. See Dependencies.

docs.title: "Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement elapid"
docs.text: This usually means the QGIS Python is older than 3.9. QMaxent requires Python ≥ 3.9 because that is the floor elapid sets. Upgrade QGIS to the LTR ≥ 3.34 release; the bundled Python is 3.9+.

docs.title: Plugin Manager shows QMaxent but "Install" is greyed out
docs.text: You probably already have QMaxent installed in a user plugin directory and the Plugin Manager is showing the system package list. Check Plugins → Manage and Install Plugins → Installed — uninstall the older copy first, then re-install the latest.

docs.title: "ValueError: All presence points fell on NoData cells"
docs.text:
The presence layer's CRS or extent does not overlap the raster stack. Check on ① Data:

  1. Click on a presence point in QGIS to read its coordinates.
  2. Click on a raster cell in roughly the same area to confirm the raster has a value there.
  3. If they disagree, the layer is misprojected — re-export the presence layer with the rasters' CRS using Vector → Save Layer As….

docs.title: "Convergence not reached after 500 iterations"
docs.text:
The model could not find a likelihood maximum within the iteration cap. Three common causes:

  • Too few presences for the chosen feature classes. Switch to Auto mode on ② Parameters and the maxnet rule will simplify the feature set automatically.
  • Highly collinear variables. Use Jackknife Importance on the results tab to identify near-zero contributors and drop them.
  • Categorical variable with very rare classes. Re-bin the rare classes into an Other category before modeling.

docs.title: "These rasters cannot be aligned because of their coordinate reference system"
docs.text: Check Raster Consistency found a raster with no CRS, or with a local (engineering) CRS without a datum, which PROJ cannot reproject. This is typical of a .prj file that only names a projection, such as NAD83(NSRS2007) / Michigan South. The message names the file and, when possible, the matching EPSG code. In the Layers panel, right-click the raster, choose Layer CRS > Set Layer CRS..., pick the correct CRS, and run the check again; Check and Harmonize to Folder... then use that CRS. See ① Data tab.

docs.title: "QMaxent uses one raster band per environmental variable"
docs.text: A raster in the list has several bands. Split it into single-band files, for example with Processing > GDAL > Raster conversion > Rearrange bands (one band per output), and add the single-band files instead.

docs.title: "Grid mismatch — CRS, extent, resolution differ across rasters"
docs.text: This is the Check Raster Consistency failure mode. Click Harmonize to Folder… and let QMaxent reproject every raster to the highest-resolution one. The Ariolimax worked example walks through this.

docs.title: Training is very slow (>10 minutes for 100 presences)
docs.text:
Two common causes:

  • Very large raster stack (e.g. 30-m resolution over a continental extent). Background-point extraction is the bottleneck. Either reduce the raster resolution to a value appropriate for the species' home- range size, or restrict the analysis to a relevant ROI by clipping the rasters first.
  • Too many background points. The default 10,000 is appropriate for most studies; a value of 50,000+ rarely helps and slows the run proportionally.

docs.title: Spatial projection is fast but uses lots of RAM
docs.text: Projection loads the full raster stack into memory cell-by-cell. For a continental 1-km stack of 10 variables, expect ~2 GB peak. If RAM is tight, downsample the rasters before projection — projection at the training resolution is methodologically defensible (Elith, Kearney & Phillips 2010).

docs.title: "Why are some cells in my projection NoData when the rasters cover them?"
docs.text:
The unified preflight dialog auto-masks two cell categories to NoData (a categorical class missing from the training data no longer makes the projection fail; see ④ Results tab):

  1. Categorical class codes that did not appear during training.
  2. Cells where any continuous variable lies outside its training range — only when the relevant safety mask is enabled.

This is intentional (Elith, Kearney & Phillips 2010) — extrapolation beyond the training domain is undefined and should be flagged, not silently filled in.

docs.title: Can I project onto a different region than I trained on?
docs.text: Yes — but the preflight dialog will flag every continuous variable whose new-region range exceeds its training range, and will auto-mask unseen categorical codes. Read the dialog before clicking Yes; treat any reported extrapolation as a finding to discuss in the paper.

docs.title: The output cloglog values look uniformly low
docs.text: Probably normal — cloglog values (Phillips et al. 2017) are calibrated as "probability of presence given a typical sample of the species at this location", and that is genuinely low (<0.5) over most of any species' range. The peaks (0.7+) are what matter; the absolute scale is not directly comparable across species or studies.

docs.title: How to ask a good question
docs.text:
When opening an issue on GitHub, please include:

  1. The QMaxent version (Plugins → Manage and Install Plugins → Installed, or metadata.txt).
  2. The QGIS version (Help → About).
  3. The exact error message (copy from the Training tab log or the QGIS Python console).
  4. A minimum reproducer — ideally a small dataset that triggers the problem, or screenshots of the ① Data and ② Parameters tabs so we can see the configuration.

The fastest issues to resolve are the ones that ship with everything a maintainer needs to recreate the failure on their own machine.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: QMaxent installs as a regular QGIS plugin. After the plugin itself is in place, a one-time dependency setup downloads the Python libraries Maxent needs into a separate QMaxent folder that does not affect your system Python or QGIS itself. On Linux and macOS this folder is a Python virtual environment; on Windows it is a plain package folder filled by the QGIS Python's own pip (see Dependencies).

docs.title: System requirements
docs.text:
• QGIS 3.44 LTR or later
  • Operating system: Windows 10/11, macOS 12+, or any modern Linux distribution
  • Disk space: about 600 MB free for the QMaxent package folder
  • Internet access is required only on first run to download the Python dependencies; routine model fitting and projection run fully offline.

docs.title: Install from the QGIS Plugin Repository
docs.text: QMaxent is published on the official QGIS Plugin Repository.

docs.title: Step 1. Open the Plugin Manager
docs.text:
1. Open the Plugins menu.
  2. Click Manage and Install Plugins...

docs.title: Step 2. Find QMaxent and install it
docs.text:
1. Make sure the All page is selected on the left.
  2. Type QMaxent in the search box.
  3. Click QMaxent in the result list. Its description appears on the right.
  4. Click Install Plugin. When the installation ends, click Close.

docs.title: Step 3. Find the QMaxent menu
docs.text:
1. Open the Plugins menu again.
  2. Point to QMaxent. Three entries appear.
  3. QMaxent Dependencies opens the dependency setup described in the next chapter.
Menu item What it does QMaxent Analysis Opens the Analysis dock, where all modelling happens QMaxent Dependencies Opens the dependency setup (next chapter) Download Example Dataset... Downloads the example data used in this manual (see Example datasets)

docs.title: Verifying the installation
docs.text:
Right after the installation, QMaxent opens two panels on the right side of QGIS: QMaxent Dependencies at the top and the QMaxent Analysis dock below it.

  1. The QMaxent Dependencies panel reads Dependencies not installed the first time. That is expected: the next chapter installs them.

If the panels do not appear, choose Plugins → QMaxent → QMaxent Dependencies. If that opens, the plugin is installed correctly.

docs.title: Updating to a newer version
docs.text: When a new release ships, the QGIS Plugin Manager will mark QMaxent as upgradable. Click Upgrade Plugin in the Installed tab. Dependencies generally do not need to be reinstalled across patch releases (0.1.x → 0.1.y). When the package list or the installation method changes, the Dependencies dialog reports that the dependencies need updating; click Install / Update Dependencies once more. This is the case when you upgrade to 0.2.0 on Windows, because 0.2.0 changed how packages are installed there.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
QMaxent does not appear in the search results

Make sure your QGIS version is 3.44 or later (Help → About QGIS). On older versions QMaxent is filtered out as incompatible. Also confirm the Show experimental plugins option in Settings is set to your preference — QMaxent's stable releases do not require it.

Plugin installs but the menu entry does not appear

Restart QGIS. Some QGIS versions require a restart for top-level menu entries from new plugins to register.

Windows: installation stops with 'ensurepip ... returned non-zero exit status 1'

QMaxent 0.1.x created a Python virtual environment, and this step fails with QGIS 3.44.15 and later on Windows. QMaxent 0.2.0 no longer needs a virtual environment on Windows: it installs the packages with the QGIS Python's own pip into the QMaxent package folder. Upgrade the plugin to 0.2.0 or later and click Install / Update Dependencies again. Details are in Dependencies.

Corporate proxy or restricted network

The plugin install itself uses QGIS's network stack and respects QGIS's proxy settings. The dependency installer (next chapter) downloads from PyPI; if your organisation blocks PyPI, ask your network administrator to allow pypi.org and files.pythonhosted.org.

Once installed, continue to Dependencies.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: QMaxent is a QGIS plugin that brings the full Maxent species distribution modeling (SDM) workflow inside the GIS. From a single docked panel you can choose presence points, register environmental rasters, train a regularised Maxent model, evaluate it with spatial cross-validation, project it across the landscape, and generate field-ready candidate survey sites — without leaving QGIS or writing a line of code.

docs.title: What is QMaxent
docs.text: Under the hood, QMaxent wraps the elapid Python library (Anderson 2023). Elapid implements the maxnet algorithm — a penalised Poisson formulation that is provably equivalent to the original Maxent model on a sufficient sample of background points (Fithian & Hastie 2013) — using the lasso-regularised generalised linear model machinery of glmnet (Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010). The user-facing model is the same Maxent that the broader SDM literature has used since Phillips, Anderson & Schapire (2006); the difference is the surrounding tooling, not the inferential engine.

docs.title: Intended users
docs.text:
QMaxent is for ecologists, conservation planners, and biogeographers who:

  • Already use QGIS for spatial analysis and want SDM as an integrated step rather than a separate Java GUI
  • Need cross-validated, spatially honest performance estimates rather than an over-optimistic in-sample AUC (Roberts et al. 2017)
  • Want their results to be reproducible — fixed seeds, configuration written to a multi-sheet Excel supplement, model serialised as a portable .pkl
  • Work bilingually (Korean / English) and need a UI in their language

You do not need to know Python. You do need a working knowledge of vector points and raster layers in QGIS, and enough domain knowledge of your study system to choose appropriate environmental predictors.

docs.title: How it compares to other SDM tools
docs.text:
Tool Interface Engine Status QMaxent QGIS plugin elapid (maxnet, Python) Active, this manual Java MaxEnt Standalone Java GUI Original Maxent Stable; broadly used ENMeval (R) R package maxnet / dismo Strong CV / tuning support (Muscarella et al. 2014) Wallace Shiny web app Multiple (incl. maxnet) Reproducibility focus (Kass et al. 2018) dismo (R) R package Multiple SDM algorithms Mature; broad ecosystem

QMaxent occupies the same conceptual niche as the Java MaxEnt GUI for QGIS users, with the added benefit of a modern Python runtime that ships with QGIS, an integrated raster-consistency preflight, and built-in spatial cross-validation. The Pitta nympha worked example reproduces a published Java MaxEnt analysis in QMaxent and discusses where the two pipelines agree or diverge.

docs.title: Methodological lineage
docs.text:
QMaxent's defaults follow the recommendations of:

  • Phillips, Anderson & Schapire (2006), Phillips & Dudík (2008), and Phillips et al. (2017) for the core Maxent formulation, regularization, and cloglog output transform.
  • Elith et al. (2011) and Merow, Smith & Silander (2013) for practitioner guidance on inputs and settings.
  • The maxnet R package (Phillips et al. 2017) for the default rule that selects feature classes by sample size. It is a default, not a guarantee of the best model (Merow, Smith & Silander 2013; Radosavljevic & Anderson 2014).
  • Roberts et al. (2017) for spatial cross-validation as the default evaluation method.

Every default in the plugin can be overridden in the ② Parameters tab. Full citations are in References.

docs.title: Methodological background
docs.text: This chapter collects the why behind the how — the academic reasoning that justifies QMaxent's defaults. It is intended for users who want to understand or cite the model choices, not for first-time users (who should read the User guide chapters first).

docs.title: Maxent and the principle of maximum entropy
docs.text:
Maxent fits the maximum-entropy distribution consistent with the empirical moments observed at the presence locations (Phillips, Anderson & Schapire 2006). Intuitively: among all distributions over the study area that produce the same average value of each environmental variable as the presence sample, the maximum- entropy distribution is the least informative — the one that adds no assumptions beyond what the data actually says.

The estimator is mathematically equivalent to a regularized inhomogeneous Poisson point-process model fit to the presence-background contrast (Fithian & Hastie 2013) — and that equivalence is what elapid's implementation exploits to delegate the optimisation to scikit-learn's logistic-regression routines (Anderson 2023; Pedregosa et al. 2011).

docs.title: The maxnet default rule for feature selection
docs.text:
The Maxent feature classes (Linear, Quadratic, Product, Hinge, Threshold) trade off flexibility against over-fit risk. maxent.jar and its R counterpart maxnet both choose default feature classes from the number of presence points. QMaxent's Auto (maxnet default rule by sample size) mode applies the maxnet default (Phillips et al. 2017; maxnet.formula(classes = "default")):

Presences Feature classes fewer than 10 L 10 to 14 L, Q 15 to 79 L, Q, H 80 or more L, Q, P, H

Unlike the maxent.jar rule, which QMaxent used up to v0.1.x, the maxnet default never adds threshold features. This matters for QMaxent's engine: elapid fits the model with scikit-learn, which applies one regularization strength to all features, whereas maxent.jar regularizes each feature class separately. Under a single penalty the many step-shaped threshold features overfit. On the Bradypus benchmark (random 10-fold CV), the test AUC was 0.873 with LQPHT and 0.890 with LQPH, against 0.895 for maxent.jar with LQPHT. Threshold features are still available under Manual selection.

The rule is a default, not a guarantee of the best model. The most suitable feature classes and regularization depend on the data (Merow, Smith & Silander 2013; Radosavljevic & Anderson 2014). For a publication, compare alternatives with Manual selection and spatial cross-validation, or with a model-selection tool such as ENMeval (Muscarella et al. 2014).

docs.title: Why spatial cross-validation matters
docs.text:
Random K-Fold CV gives over-optimistic AUCs on spatial data because random folds are likely to contain points geographically adjacent to training points. Spatial autocorrelation makes the held-out points trivially predictable.

Roberts et al. 2017 demonstrate this empirically across many SDM benchmarks: random-K-Fold AUCs systematically over-estimate the performance you would actually see on a new region by 0.05–0.15. They recommend spatially-blocked CV as the default for any spatial model.

QMaxent therefore defaults to Geographic K-Fold (k = 5, fixed seed) — the recommended Roberts et al. design. Random K-Fold is offered only to allow exact reproduction of older studies.

docs.title: Pooled vs per-fold AUC
docs.text:
Two summary statistics across folds are commonly reported:

  • Per-fold AUC then averaged — compute AUC inside each fold, average across folds, report mean ± SD.
  • Pooled AUC — concatenate all held-out predictions across folds and compute a single AUC.

QMaxent reports the per-fold mean ± SD as the headline number because it carries the across-fold variance, which is itself an informative diagnostic — high variance signals that the model's geographic transferability is unstable. The pooled-AUC alternative is included in Table 3 of the XLSX as a secondary metric.

docs.title: Jackknife variable importance
docs.text:
The classical Maxent jackknife (Phillips, Anderson & Schapire 2006) fits, for each variable, two extra models: one with that variable alone (with-only) and one with that variable removed (without). The drop in test AUC from full to without identifies variables whose unique contribution is hard to recover from the others.

QMaxent reports four AUCs per variable (only-train, only-test, without-train, without-test) plus the test-side drop column, sorted by descending drop so the most uniquely-informative variables are at the top. This is the format used in the published Maxent literature since Phillips et al. 2006.

docs.title: Permutation importance and its evaluation data
docs.text:
Permutation importance shuffles one variable at a time and measures the drop in AUC. The result depends on the data the AUC is computed on, so QMaxent lets you choose it (Evaluate on on the ② Parameters tab):

  • Training data (maxent.jar convention) (default): the full model on all training presences and background points. This is how maxent.jar computes permutation importance, so rankings can be compared directly with maxent.jar studies.
  • Held-out CV test folds (all folds pooled): each fold model on its own test fold, with the results of all folds pooled. This measures how much predictive performance at new locations depends on each variable. It needs K-Fold or Checkerboard cross-validation.

Up to v0.1.x QMaxent used the test data of the first CV fold only, which made rankings unstable and not comparable with maxent.jar.

docs.title: Threshold methods (MTP / T10 / MaxSSS)
docs.text:
When you need a binary suitable/unsuitable map (e.g. for reserve-design applications), you must choose a threshold of the cloglog output. The SDM literature standardises on three options (Liu, Newell & White 2013):

  • MTP — Minimum Training Presence — the lowest cloglog value at any training presence. Most permissive; favours sensitivity.
  • T10 — 10th percentile training presence — drops the bottom 10% of training presences as outliers. The classical Java-MaxEnt default.
  • MaxSSS — Max Sensitivity + Specificity — the threshold that maximises the sum of sensitivity and specificity on the training ROC. Best calibration in most published comparisons.

QMaxent reports all three thresholds in Table 3 of the XLSX export. Choose MaxSSS unless you are reproducing a Java-MaxEnt study (T10) or have a specific reason to prefer permissive (MTP) or strict classification.

docs.title: Output transforms compared
docs.text:
Three output transforms are available on Spatial Projection:

Transform Range Interpretation cloglog 0–1 Probability of presence given a typical sample, Phillips et al. 2017 recommended default logistic 0–1 Older, Phillips & Dudík 2008 parameterisation; still used in some baselines raw unbounded Unnormalised exponential output; advanced post-processing

QMaxent defaults to cloglog because it is the form Phillips et al. 2017 explicitly recommend as the modern default and because its "probability of presence" interpretation is the most directly communicable to non-modelling stakeholders.

docs.title: Treatment of categorical variables
docs.text:
Java MaxEnt encodes categorical rasters via the raster's attribute table; elapid encodes them via one-hot expansion internally (Anderson 2023). The two approaches are equivalent for training but diverge at projection time when the raster contains class codes the model has not seen during training:

  • Java MaxEnt silently maps unseen codes to a random class, producing arbitrary suitability values at affected cells.
  • QMaxent detects unseen codes via the unified preflight dialog and auto-masks them to NoData rather than extrapolating. If an unseen class still reaches the model, the projection does not fail (since v0.2.0): those cells get no categorical contribution, as in maxent.jar.

This is the recommended practice (Elith, Kearney & Phillips 2010) — extrapolation beyond the training domain is fundamentally undefined and should be flagged, not silently filled in.

docs.title: Bias correction
docs.text:
When occurrences are spatially clustered (e.g. road-bias, citizen- science clusters), the model fits the bias surface as well as the species' habitat preference. Two complementary corrections exist:

  • Sample-weight down-weighting (Phillips et al. 2009) — applies fractional weights to clustered presences. QMaxent implements this as the Down-weight spatially clustered points option.
  • External KDE bias raster — a raster representing the survey effort, used as an explicit covariate. Not implemented in QMaxent v0.1.x; the closest analog is the down-weight option, which performs comparably for many published studies.

For a more comprehensive treatment, Boria et al. 2014 recommend spatial thinning of the presence layer before modeling as a complementary step — implementable in QGIS via the NNJoin plugin or the standalone spThin tool.

docs.title: Why these choices
docs.text: The defaults assembled in QMaxent are the union of (a) what the benchmark literature shows works well across many species and study areas, and (b) what minimises the silent-failure modes documented in Roberts et al. 2017, Araújo et al. 2019, and Elith, Kearney & Phillips 2010. Diverging from them is sometimes the right move for a specific study; the Pitta nympha worked example shows what that looks like for the LQH/RM=4 fixed-hyperparameter setting of Lee et al. 2025.

docs.title: ② Parameters tab
docs.text: The Parameters tab controls the modeling and evaluation settings: which Maxent feature classes to allow, the regularization multiplier, the spatial cross-validation method, and where to write outputs. Defaults follow established Maxent practice; this chapter explains what each control does and when to override the default.

docs.title: Step 1. Check the main settings
docs.text:
1. Feature Types: keep Auto (maxnet default rule by sample size) unless you have a reason to choose the feature classes yourself.
  2. Regularization: the Regularization multiplier controls how smooth the model is. Larger values give simpler models.
  3. Spatial evaluation: the Method used to test the model, the number of Folds, and Fix random seed for repeatable results.

docs.title: Step 2. (Optional) Choose the feature classes yourself
docs.text:
1. Select Manual selection.
  2. Tick the feature classes to use: Linear, Quadratic, Hinge, Product and Threshold.

docs.title: Step 3. (Optional) Choose another evaluation method
docs.text: 1. Open the Method list. Geographic K-Fold is the default and the safest choice for most data. The other methods are described in Spatial cross-validation.

docs.title: Step 4. Check the importance options and the output files
docs.text:
1. Advanced: hinge and threshold knots, Add presences to background and Down-weight spatially clustered points. The defaults suit most data.
  2. Fix random seed keeps the folds and the background sample the same from run to run.
  3. Jackknife variable importance fits extra models to measure each variable. It makes the run longer.
  4. Permutation importance measures how much the model gets worse when each variable is shuffled.
  5. Output Files: where the model (.pkl) and the results workbook (.xlsx) are saved. Click ... to change the paths.

Then click ▶ Run Maxent at the bottom of the dock.

docs.title: Feature Types
docs.text:
Maxent's "features" are the basis functions it uses to express the response of suitability to each environmental variable (Phillips, Anderson & Schapire 2006; Phillips et al. 2017). The five classes (LQPHT) are:

Feature Symbol What it captures Linear L Monotonic linear response Quadratic Q Optimum-shaped (∩) or U-shaped (∪) response Product P Pairwise interactions between two variables Hinge H Piecewise-linear "kink" — sharp changes at threshold values Threshold T Step-function — a hard cut-off at some value

QMaxent offers two modes:

  • Auto (maxnet default rule by sample size) (default): uses the default feature classes of maxnet, the R implementation of Maxent by its authors (Phillips et al. 2017; maxnet.formula(classes = "default")), based on the number of presence points:

    Presences Feature classes fewer than 10 L 10 to 14 LQ 15 to 79 LQH 80 or more LQPH

    Threshold features are not added automatically. - Manual selection: tick any subset of LQPHT. The boxes start with L, Q, P and H ticked and Threshold unticked. Use this to compare alternatives or to reproduce a published study that fixed a particular feature combination (e.g. the Pitta nympha example fixes feature classes to LQH to match Lee et al. 2025).

Why Auto no longer adds threshold features

Up to v0.1.x, Auto followed the maxent.jar rule and added threshold features (LQPHT) for 80 or more presences. With elapid's scikit-learn backend, every feature gets the same regularization strength, while maxent.jar regularizes each feature class separately. Threshold features then overfit. On the Bradypus benchmark (random 10-fold CV), the test AUC was 0.873 with LQPHT and 0.890 with LQPH; maxent.jar with LQPHT reached 0.895. v0.2.0 therefore follows the maxnet default, which does not use threshold features. They remain available under Manual selection.

Auto is a default, not the best model

The rule gives a reasonable starting point, but the most suitable feature classes depend on the data (Merow, Smith & Silander 2013; Radosavljevic & Anderson 2014). To choose them, compare alternatives with Manual selection and spatial cross-validation, or use a model-selection tool such as ENMeval (Muscarella et al. 2014). Be aware that repeatedly tuning settings against random (non-spatial) CV gives optimistic AUCs (Roberts et al. 2017).

docs.title: Regularization multiplier
docs.text: Maxent fits a regularized maximum-entropy distribution — the regularization multiplier (RM) controls how strongly the fit is penalised for complexity. - RM = 1 (default) — the value Phillips & Dudík 2008 showed yields the best held-out AUC across the full Maxent benchmark. - RM > 1 (e.g. 2–4) — smoother responses, less over-fit, lower training AUC but often higher CV AUC. Use when occurrences are small in number, spatially clustered, or biased. - RM < 1 — only justified by a formal hyperparameter search such as ENMeval (Muscarella et al. 2014) or Wallace (Kass et al. 2018).

docs.title: Spatial cross-validation
docs.text:
A drop-down picks the spatial CV scheme used to split presences into folds:

Method Best for Reference Geographic K-Fold (default) General-purpose Roberts et al. 2017 Random K-Fold Reproducing studies that used random splits Phillips et al. 2017 Checkerboard Strong spatial autocorrelation in presences Muscarella et al. 2014 Buffered Leave-One-Out Very small datasets (n < 30) Hijmans 2012; Valavi et al. 2019

The default Geographic K-Fold (k = 5, fixed seed = 42) strikes a balance recommended by Roberts et al. 2017: geographic blocks break the spatial-autocorrelation cheating that random K-Fold permits, yet keep the held-out folds large enough for a stable AUC.

The fixed seed makes every run bit-for-bit reproducible — a property cited as essential by the SDM-best-practice review of Araújo et al. 2019.

docs.title: Jackknife variable importance
docs.text:
When the Jackknife checkbox is on, QMaxent fits 2 × N additional single-predictor and leave-one-out models to estimate each variable's unique contribution. The cost is roughly 2 × N × training time; for the Bradypus dataset (9 variables, 116 presences) this adds about 30 seconds.

Jackknife output is rendered in two places: 1. The ④ Results → Jackknife Importance sub-tab as a paired-bar plot. 2. Table 4 of the exported XLSX workbook, with all four AUC columns plus computed Train AUC drop and Test AUC drop.

The interpretation follows the original Phillips, Anderson & Schapire 2006 reading: "with-only" bars show univariate signal; "without" bars show how dependent the full model is on each variable.

docs.title: Permutation importance
docs.text:
When Permutation importance is ticked, QMaxent shuffles the values of each variable in turn and measures the drop in AUC (scikit-learn permutation_importance, Repeats shuffles per variable, default 10). The drops are reported as a percentage of the total, the convention of maxent.jar. The Evaluate on drop-down sets which data the AUC drop is measured on:

Option What is evaluated Use it to Training data (maxent.jar convention) (default) The full model on all training presences and background points, as maxent.jar does Compare variable rankings with maxent.jar studies Held-out CV test folds (all folds pooled) Each cross-validation fold model on its own test fold; the results of all folds are pooled See how much predictive performance at new locations depends on each variable

The held-out option needs Geographic K-Fold, Random K-Fold or Checkerboard cross-validation. With no CV or with Buffered LOO, QMaxent falls back to the training data and says so in the log. (v0.1.x used only the first CV fold, which made rankings unstable.) The training log and the model card record which option was used.

Permutation importance is fast (no refitting), but it can underestimate the importance of variables that are correlated with others. Read it together with the jackknife.

docs.title: Output paths
docs.text:
Two file paths default to a qmaxent_output/ subdirectory of the current QGIS project:

  • Model file (.pkl) — the serialised trained model, reloadable from the Data tab. QMaxent also writes <model>_model_card.json and <model>_coefficients.csv next to it. See Saving and reusing models for these files and the security note on Python pickle files.
  • Results workbook (.xlsx) — multi-sheet supplementary table. See Exporting results for the sheet-by-sheet layout.

Clear either field to skip writing that file. The model object remains in memory for the rest of the session even when not saved to disk.

docs.title: Advanced options
docs.text:
A collapsible Advanced section exposes:

  • Fix random seed (default on, value 42): one seed for every random step of a run, that is CV fold partitions, hold-out splits, permutation shuffles, survey-site shuffling and, since v0.2.0, the background-point draw (v0.1.x drew a different background on every run). Background points are drawn from the first raster in the ① Data list, so keep the raster order the same to reproduce a run exactly. The seed value is written to the Overview sheet of results.xlsx and to the model card.
  • Down-weight spatially clustered points — applies the Phillips et al. 2009 sample-bias correction by giving duplicates and very-near-duplicate occurrences less weight in the likelihood. Recommended whenever the presence layer was assembled from ad-hoc records (museum specimens, citizen-science sightings, etc.).
  • Add presences to background — on by default, matching Java MaxEnt convention. Required for the Maxent likelihood to be well-defined (Phillips & Dudík 2008).

docs.title: Next
docs.text: When everything is configured, click ▶ Run Maxent at the dock footer. Focus shifts to the ③ Training tab.

docs.title: ⑤ Survey Site Selection
docs.text: The fifth tab, ⑤ Survey Site Selection (called Priority Sites for Survey before v0.2.0), turns a habitat-suitability raster into a field-ready list of candidate survey sites. Field surveys usually have one of two purposes: looking for new populations, or checking the model in the field. QMaxent supports both with separate sampling designs grounded in the survey-design literature.

docs.title: Step 1. Choose the purpose and the settings
docs.text:
1. Survey purpose: High-suitability search looks for new populations in suitable, unsurveyed places. Gradient-stratified sampling checks the model along its suitability gradient (Step 2).
  2. High-suitability search settings: the Minimum suitability and the Sampling order (Random or Top-N (highest first)).
  3. Sampling strategy: the number of sites and the minimum distances (in metres) from known presences and between sites.
  4. ▶ Select Survey Sites runs the selection.

docs.title: Step 2. (Validation surveys) Use gradient-stratified sampling
docs.text:
1. Select Gradient-stratified sampling.
  2. Gradient-stratified sampling settings: the Threshold method sets the lowest suitability included. Cells above it are split into four suitability bands and sites are spread over the bands.

docs.title: Step 3. Addresses and the output file
docs.text:
1. Reverse geocoding: Add administrative address (OpenStreetMap) writes the address of each site. Address language chooses local names or another language. It needs an internet connection.
  2. Output: the GeoPackage path and Auto-add to QGIS project.

docs.title: Step 4. Run and check the sites
docs.text:
1. The progress bar.
  2. The status line, for example the reverse geocoding count.
  1. The status line reports how many sites were selected and where the file was saved.
  1. The survey sites layer is added to the Layers panel.

docs.title: Survey purpose
docs.text:
Pick one:

Mode Goal Reference High-suitability search Look for new populations in unsurveyed high-suitability areas Williams et al. 2009 Gradient-stratified sampling Check the model along its suitability gradient: does observed occurrence follow the predicted suitability? Rhoden, Peterman & Taylor 2017

The two modes ask very different questions of the same map, so they sample it differently:

  • High-suitability search (formerly Discovery mode) samples sites only from a band of high suitability, away from known occurrences. These are the most promising places to find the species where it has not been recorded yet.
  • Gradient-stratified sampling (formerly Validation mode) splits the cells above a threshold into four suitability quartiles and draws the same number of sites from each. Lower-suitability sites are included on purpose, so the field results can show whether the species is found more often where the model predicts higher suitability.

docs.title: Mode settings
docs.text: Only the settings group of the selected mode is shown.

docs.title: High-suitability search settings
docs.text: Control What it does Minimum suitability Cells with suitability at or above this value form the candidate pool. It is filled in automatically as 0.9 × the maximum of the prediction raster when the raster is selected; you can type another value. Sampling order: Random (default) Draws sites at random from the candidate pool. This gives an unbiased sample within the high-suitability band. Sampling order: Top-N (highest first) Takes the cells with the highest suitability first. Use it when you want to maximise the expected hit rate.

docs.title: Gradient-stratified sampling settings
docs.text:
Control What it does Threshold method Sets the lower bound of the sampling frame: 10th percentile training presence (T10; Pearson 2007) (default), Minimum training presence (MTP; Pearson 2007), Maximum sum of sensitivity + specificity (MaxSSS; Liu 2013), or Custom value... Computed threshold value The threshold computed from the training data for the chosen method (editable only for Custom value...)

The threshold only defines the sampling frame. The cells above it are split into four quartiles of suitability, and the same number of sites is drawn from each quartile (Rhoden, Peterman & Taylor 2017). No binary suitable/unsuitable map is produced, and the threshold is not a claim that cells below it are unsuitable. Each site carries its quartile in the quartile field (0 = lowest band above the threshold, 3 = highest), and the layer is styled by quartile. In High-suitability search the field is always 0.

docs.title: Spacing constraints
docs.text:
The Sampling strategy group is shared by both modes. Besides the Number of survey sites (default 20), two distance fields define the spatial structure of the sampled set:

  • Min. distance from existing presences (m) (default 1,000) keeps candidates away from known occurrences. Set it to the species' detection radius (e.g. 1 km for a calling fairy pitta, 200 m for a slug). This prevents the algorithm from re-sampling territory already covered by earlier surveys.
  • Min. distance between sites (m) (default 500) keeps the candidate set spatially independent. A typical value is half the distance from existing presences. Spatially balanced sampling, in the sense of Stevens & Olsen 2004, is approximated by setting this value to the nearest-neighbour distance you want in the final set.

QMaxent enforces both constraints exactly: candidates are dropped, not moved, when a constraint is violated, so the surviving set is always within the specification. If the candidate pool cannot supply the requested number of sites under these constraints, QMaxent returns the sites it found and reports the actual count.

docs.title: Reverse geocoding
docs.text:
When Add administrative address (OpenStreetMap) is ticked, QMaxent calls the Nominatim service of OpenStreetMap for each site. No API key is needed. Reverse geocoding works worldwide. It adds four generic OpenStreetMap address levels and the full address:

Field Address level Examples country Country Dominican Republic, South Korea province First-level administrative division a Dominican provincia, a Korean province, a US state city_county Municipality a Dominican municipio, a Korean city or county district Locality a suburb, village, neighbourhood or hamlet display_name Full address text returned by Nominatim

A level that OpenStreetMap does not hold for a location is left blank.

Address language sets the language of the names:

  • Local names (default): each country's own names, for example Spanish names in the Dominican Republic and Korean names in Korea.
  • QGIS interface language: the language of your QGIS interface, with English as a fallback.
  • English: English names where OpenStreetMap has them.

The resulting GeoPackage is directly usable for permit applications and field-team coordination, which matters in jurisdictions where survey access requires prior notice to the local administration.

Requests are limited to one per second to comply with Nominatim's fair-use policy, so 20 sites take about 20 seconds. For 30 or more sites QMaxent first shows the expected time; for large sets, untick the option or select the sites in smaller batches. Results carry the attribution © OpenStreetMap contributors.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
After clicking ▶ Select Survey Sites, QMaxent writes:

  • survey_sites.gpkg (default name, in the QMaxent output folder): a GeoPackage point layer with the fields id, lat, lon, suitability, quartile and the address fields above. With Auto-add to QGIS project ticked, it is added to the map as the layer Survey sites.

If the output GeoPackage already exists, it is replaced, and any layer of the current project that reads it is removed first. If another program holds the file open, QMaxent writes to the next free name instead, such as survey_sites_1.gpkg, and reports the name it used.

The training thresholds (MTP, T10, MaxSSS) that Gradient-stratified sampling can use are also recorded in the model card (<model>_model_card.json, see Saving and reusing models).

The sites are immediately ready for export to mobile-GIS apps such as QField, Mergin Maps, or Locus Map for offline field use.

docs.title: Choosing parameter values
docs.text:
Some practical starting points:

  • Number of survey sites: 20–30 per species per season is a typical field-survey budget for a single team (Robinson et al. 2018).
  • Min. distance from existing presences: the species' typical home-range diameter is a good starting point. Too small and you re-sample known sites; too large and you push candidates into marginal habitat.
  • Minimum suitability (High-suitability search): the automatic value (0.9 × raster maximum) gives a focused search; lower it to widen the candidate pool when too few sites satisfy the spacing rules.
  • Threshold method (Gradient-stratified sampling): T10 or MTP give a wide frame that includes lower-suitability cells; MaxSSS gives a narrower one.

docs.title: Worked applications
docs.text:
• The Bradypus example walks through both modes at continental scale.
  • The Pitta nympha example shows a High-suitability search at municipality scale, with reverse-geocoded administrative addresses ready for field permits.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Move to Saving and reusing models to learn how to share the trained model with collaborators or re-project it onto a new raster stack later.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This walkthrough takes you from a freshly installed plugin to a finished habitat-suitability map and a list of field survey sites for Bradypus variegatus, the brown-throated three-toed sloth. It is the same species the original Maxent paper used (Phillips, Anderson & Schapire 2006).

Every step shows the real QGIS screen. The red boxes and numbered circles on each picture match the numbered instructions below it, so you can follow along click by click.

Before you start

Complete Installation and Dependencies first. The QMaxent environment ready status must be shown in green before you continue.

How long does it take?

About 10 minutes in total. Most of that is the model fit in Step 9, which runs in the background while QGIS stays usable.

docs.title: Step 1. Open the example dataset downloader
docs.text:
1. Open the Plugins menu in the QGIS menu bar.
  2. Point to QMaxent.
  3. Click Download Example Dataset...

docs.title: Step 2. Choose Bradypus and download
docs.text:
1. Select Bradypus variegatus.
  2. Check the folder in Save to. The default is a qmaxent_examples folder in your home folder. Click ... to choose another place.
  3. Click Download.

The download takes a few seconds. When the message below appears, click OK.

docs.title: Step 3. Check the layers on the map
docs.text: 1. The Layers panel now lists the bradypus presence layer and the nine environmental rasters (bio1 to bio17 and biome). The blue points on the map are the 116 places where the sloth was recorded.

docs.title: Part 2. Prepare the data (① Data tab)
Step 4. Open the Analysis dock
docs.text:
Choose Plugins → QMaxent → QMaxent Analysis. The Analysis dock opens on the right side of QGIS.

  1. ① Data: choose the presence points and the environmental rasters.
  2. ② Parameters: set how the model is fitted and evaluated.
  3. ③ Training: follow the model fit and read the log.
  4. ④ Results: look at response curves and variable importance, and make the suitability map.
  5. ⑤ Survey Site Selection: pick field survey sites from the map.
  6. ▶ Run Maxent starts the model fit. You use it once the first two tabs are ready.

Work through the tabs from left to right.

docs.title: Step 5. Choose the presence points
docs.text:
1. In Presence Points Layer, choose bradypus. The line below it reads 116 presence points loaded.
  2. Open point file... loads a point file (GeoPackage, shapefile and others) that is not yet in your project.
  3. Load CSV (X/Y columns)... loads a table with coordinate columns. You do not need either button for this example.

docs.title: Step 6. Add the environmental rasters
docs.text:
1. Click Add from project.
  2. Every raster in the project appears in the list. The button on the right of each row shows whether QMaxent treats the raster as [continuous] or [categorical]. Click it to change the type. Scroll down the list and check that biome is marked [categorical], because its values are class codes, not amounts.

docs.title: Step 7. Check that the rasters line up
docs.text:
1. Click Check Raster Consistency.
  2. The status line turns green: ✓ All 9 rasters share grid (CRS: EPSG:4326, resolution: 0.5 × 0.5). If it turns red instead, see Fixing rasters that do not line up.

docs.title: Part 3. Fit the model (② Parameters and ③ Training)
Step 8. Review the parameters
docs.text:
Click the ② Parameters tab. For this first run, keep the defaults.

  1. Feature Types: Auto (maxnet default rule by sample size) chooses the feature classes from the number of presences. With 116 records it uses linear, quadratic, product and hinge (LQPH).
  2. Regularization: a multiplier of 1.00 is the usual starting value.
  3. Spatial evaluation: Geographic K-Fold with 5 folds checks the model on areas it did not see during fitting. Fix random seed: 42 makes the run repeatable.

These defaults are a sensible starting point (Phillips & Dudík 2008; Phillips et al. 2017), not a guarantee of the best model for your own data.

docs.title: Step 9. Run Maxent
docs.text:
Click ▶ Run Maxent at the bottom of the dock. QMaxent switches to the ③ Training tab.

  1. The progress bar shows how far the run is.
  2. The line under it names the current step.
  3. The log records every step as it happens.

When the run ends, the tab looks like this:

  1. The status line reports the result.
